title: Physical quantities as magnitude and unit
statement: understand that all physical quantities consist of a numerical magnitude and a unit

title: Estimating physical quantities
statement: make reasonable estimates of physical quantities included within the syllabus

title: SI base quantities and units
statement: recall the following SI base quantities and their units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K)

title: Expressing derived units
statement: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate

title: Checking homogeneity with SI units
statement: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

title: SI unit prefixes
statement: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

title: Systematic and random errors
statement: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements

title: Precision versus accuracy
statement: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy

title: Combining uncertainties in derived quantities
statement: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

title: Scalar and vector quantities
statement: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus

title: Adding and subtracting coplanar vectors
statement: add and subtract coplanar vectors

title: Resolving a vector into components
statement: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

title: Defining distance, speed, velocity, acceleration
statement: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

title: Graphs of motion quantities
statement: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

title: Displacement from a velocity-time graph
statement: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

title: Velocity from a displacement-time graph
statement: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

title: Acceleration from a velocity-time graph
statement: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

title: Deriving the suvat equations
statement: derive, from the definitions of velocity and acceleration, equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line

title: Solving uniformly accelerated motion problems
statement: solve problems using equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line, including the motion of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field without air resistance

title: Measuring the acceleration of free fall
statement: describe an experiment to determine the acceleration of free fall using a falling object

title: Projectile motion in two dimensions
statement: describe and explain motion due to a uniform velocity in one direction and a uniform acceleration in a perpendicular direction

title: Mass as resistance to motion
statement: understand that mass is the property of an object that resists change in motion

title: Newton's second law, F = ma
statement: recall $F = ma$ and solve problems using it, understanding that acceleration and resultant force are always in the same direction

title: Defining linear momentum
statement: define and use linear momentum as the product of mass and velocity

title: Force as rate of change of momentum
statement: define and use force as rate of change of momentum

title: Newton's three laws of motion
statement: state and apply each of Newton's laws of motion

title: Weight as a gravitational force
statement: describe and use the concept of weight as the effect of a gravitational field on a mass and recall that the weight of an object is equal to the product of its mass and the acceleration of free fall

title: Friction and drag forces
statement: show a qualitative understanding of frictional forces and viscous/drag forces including air resistance (no treatment of the coefficients of friction and viscosity is required, and a simple model of drag force increasing as speed increases is sufficient)

title: Falling motion with air resistance
statement: describe and explain qualitatively the motion of objects in a uniform gravitational field with air resistance

title: Reaching terminal velocity
statement: understand that objects moving against a resistive force may reach a terminal (constant) velocity

title: Conservation of momentum
statement: state the principle of conservation of momentum

title: Solving collision problems with momentum
statement: apply the principle of conservation of momentum to solve simple problems, including elastic and inelastic interactions between objects in both one and two dimensions (knowledge of the concept of coefficient of restitution is not required)

title: Elastic collisions and kinetic energy
statement: recall that, for an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved and the relative speed of approach is equal to the relative speed of separation

title: Momentum conserved, kinetic energy may change
statement: understand that, while momentum of a system is always conserved in interactions between objects, some change in kinetic energy may take place

title: Centre of gravity
statement: understand that the weight of an object may be taken as acting at a single point known as its centre of gravity

title: Moment of a force
statement: define and apply the moment of a force

title: Couples as pure rotation forces
statement: understand that a couple is a pair of forces that acts to produce rotation only

title: Torque of a couple
statement: define and apply the torque of a couple

title: Principle of moments
statement: state and apply the principle of moments

title: Equilibrium of forces and torques
statement: understand that, when there is no resultant force and no resultant torque, a system is in equilibrium

title: Vector triangle for forces in equilibrium
statement: use a vector triangle to represent coplanar forces in equilibrium

title: Defining density
statement: define and use density

title: Defining pressure
statement: define and use pressure

title: Deriving hydrostatic pressure
statement: derive, from the definitions of pressure and density, the equation for hydrostatic pressure $\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h$

title: Using hydrostatic pressure equation
statement: use the equation $\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h$

title: Upthrust from pressure difference
statement: understand that the upthrust acting on an object in a fluid is due to a difference in hydrostatic pressure

title: Calculating upthrust, Archimedes' principle
statement: calculate the upthrust acting on an object in a fluid using the equation $F = \rho g V$ (Archimedes' principle)

title: Work done by a force
statement: understand the concept of work, and recall and use work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force

title: Conservation of energy
statement: recall and apply the principle of conservation of energy

title: Efficiency as a ratio of energies
statement: recall and understand that the efficiency of a system is the ratio of useful energy output from the system to the total energy input

title: Solving efficiency problems
statement: use the concept of efficiency to solve problems

title: Defining power
statement: define power as work done per unit time

title: Solving power problems, P = W/t
statement: solve problems using $P = W/t$

title: Deriving and using P = Fv
statement: derive $P = Fv$ and use it to solve problems

title: Deriving gravitational potential energy change
statement: derive, using $W = Fs$, the formula $\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$ for gravitational potential energy changes in a uniform gravitational field

title: Using gravitational potential energy change
statement: recall and use the formula $\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$ for gravitational potential energy changes in a uniform gravitational field

title: Deriving kinetic energy formula
statement: derive, using the equations of motion, the formula for kinetic energy $E_K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$

title: Using the kinetic energy formula
statement: recall and use $E_K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$

title: Deformation by tensile or compressive forces
statement: understand that deformation is caused by tensile or compressive forces (forces and deformations will be assumed to be in one dimension only)

title: Load, extension and limit of proportionality
statement: understand and use the terms load, extension, compression and limit of proportionality

title: Hooke's law
statement: recall and use Hooke's law

title: Spring constant, k = F/x
statement: recall and use the formula for the spring constant $k = F/x$

title: Stress, strain and Young modulus
statement: define and use the terms stress, strain and the Young modulus

title: Measuring the Young modulus of a wire
statement: describe an experiment to determine the Young modulus of a metal in the form of a wire

title: Elastic and plastic deformation
statement: understand and use the terms elastic deformation, plastic deformation and elastic limit

title: Work done from a force-extension graph
statement: understand that the area under the force–extension graph represents the work done

title: Elastic potential energy from a graph
statement: determine the elastic potential energy of a material deformed within its limit of proportionality from the area under the force–extension graph

title: Elastic potential energy formulas
statement: recall and use $E_P = \frac{1}{2}Fx = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ for a material deformed within its limit of proportionality

title: Describing wave motion
statement: describe what is meant by wave motion as illustrated by vibration in ropes, springs and ripple tanks

title: Wave terms: amplitude, period, wavelength
statement: understand and use the terms displacement, amplitude, phase difference, period, frequency, wavelength and speed

title: Using a CRO for frequency and amplitude
statement: understand the use of the time-base and y-gain of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) to determine frequency and amplitude

title: Deriving the wave equation
statement: derive, using the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength, the wave equation $v = f\lambda$

title: Using the wave equation, v = fλ
statement: recall and use $v = f\lambda$

title: Energy transfer by a progressive wave
statement: understand that energy is transferred by a progressive wave

title: Wave intensity and amplitude
statement: recall and use $\text{intensity} = \text{power}/\text{area}$ and $\text{intensity} \propto (\text{amplitude})^2$ for a progressive wave

title: Transverse versus longitudinal waves
statement: compare transverse and longitudinal waves

title: Interpreting wave graphs
statement: analyse and interpret graphical representations of transverse and longitudinal waves

title: Doppler effect, moving source
statement: understand that when a source of sound waves moves relative to a stationary observer, the observed frequency is different from the source frequency (understanding of the Doppler effect for a stationary source and a moving observer is not required)

title: Doppler effect frequency formula
statement: use the expression $f_o = \dfrac{f_s v}{v \pm v_s}$ for the observed frequency when a source of sound waves moves relative to a stationary observer
glossary: fo = fsv over v plus or minus vs

title: Electromagnetic waves travel at speed c
statement: state that all electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that travel with the same speed c in free space

title: Electromagnetic spectrum wavelength ranges
statement: recall the approximate range of wavelengths in free space of the principal regions of the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to γ-rays

title: Visible light wavelength range
statement: recall that wavelengths in the range 400–700 nm in free space are visible to the human eye

title: Polarisation of transverse waves
statement: understand that polarisation is a phenomenon associated with transverse waves

title: Malus's law for polarised intensity
statement: recall and use Malus's law ($I = I_0 \cos^2\theta$) to calculate the intensity of a plane-polarised electromagnetic wave after transmission through a polarising filter or a series of polarising filters (calculation of the effect of a polarising filter on the intensity of an unpolarised wave is not required)

title: Principle of superposition
statement: explain and use the principle of superposition

title: Demonstrating stationary waves
statement: show an understanding of experiments that demonstrate stationary waves using microwaves, stretched strings and air columns (it will be assumed that end corrections are negligible; knowledge of the concept of end corrections is not required)

title: Formation of a stationary wave
statement: explain the formation of a stationary wave using a graphical method, and identify nodes and antinodes

title: Wavelength from nodes and antinodes
statement: understand how wavelength may be determined from the positions of nodes or antinodes of a stationary wave

title: Meaning of diffraction
statement: explain the meaning of the term diffraction

title: Demonstrating diffraction
statement: show an understanding of experiments that demonstrate diffraction including the qualitative effect of the gap width relative to the wavelength of the wave; for example diffraction of water waves in a ripple tank

title: Interference and coherence
statement: understand the terms interference and coherence

title: Demonstrating two-source interference
statement: show an understanding of experiments that demonstrate two-source interference using water waves in a ripple tank, sound, light and microwaves

title: Conditions for interference fringes
statement: understand the conditions required if two-source interference fringes are to be observed

title: Double-slit interference formula
statement: recall and use $\lambda = ax/D$ for double-slit interference using light

title: Diffraction grating equation
statement: recall and use $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$

title: Measuring wavelength with a grating
statement: describe the use of a diffraction grating to determine the wavelength of light (the structure and use of the spectrometer are not included)

title: Electric current as charge flow
statement: understand that an electric current is a flow of charge carriers

title: Quantisation of charge
statement: understand that the charge on charge carriers is quantised

title: Charge, current and time, Q = It
statement: recall and use $Q = It$

title: Current in terms of charge carriers
statement: use, for a current-carrying conductor, the expression $I = Anvq$, where $n$ is the number density of charge carriers

title: Defining potential difference
statement: define the potential difference across a component as the energy transferred per unit charge

title: Using V = W/Q
statement: recall and use $V = W/Q$

title: Electrical power formulas
statement: recall and use $P = VI$, $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$

title: Defining resistance
statement: define resistance

title: Using V = IR
statement: recall and use $V = IR$

title: Sketching I-V characteristics
statement: sketch the I–V characteristics of a metallic conductor at constant temperature, a semiconductor diode and a filament lamp

title: Filament lamp resistance and temperature
statement: explain that the resistance of a filament lamp increases as current increases because its temperature increases

title: Ohm's law
statement: state Ohm's law

title: Resistivity, R = ρL/A
statement: recall and use $R = \rho L/A$

title: Light-dependent resistor behaviour
statement: understand that the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) decreases as the light intensity increases

title: Thermistor resistance and temperature
statement: understand that the resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases (it will be assumed that thermistors have a negative temperature coefficient)

title: Circuit symbols
statement: recall and use the circuit symbols shown in section 6 of this syllabus

title: Drawing and interpreting circuit diagrams
statement: draw and interpret circuit diagrams containing the circuit symbols shown in section 6 of this syllabus

title: Defining electromotive force
statement: define and use the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source as energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit

title: EMF versus potential difference
statement: distinguish between e.m.f. and potential difference (p.d.) in terms of energy considerations

title: Internal resistance and terminal pd
statement: understand the effects of the internal resistance of a source of e.m.f. on the terminal potential difference

title: Kirchhoff's first law
statement: recall Kirchhoff's first law and understand that it is a consequence of conservation of charge

title: Kirchhoff's second law
statement: recall Kirchhoff's second law and understand that it is a consequence of conservation of energy

title: Deriving series resistor combination
statement: derive, using Kirchhoff's laws, a formula for the combined resistance of two or more resistors in series

title: Using series resistor combination
statement: use the formula for the combined resistance of two or more resistors in series

title: Deriving parallel resistor combination
statement: derive, using Kirchhoff's laws, a formula for the combined resistance of two or more resistors in parallel

title: Using parallel resistor combination
statement: use the formula for the combined resistance of two or more resistors in parallel

title: Solving circuits with Kirchhoff's laws
statement: use Kirchhoff's laws to solve simple circuit problems

title: Potential divider principle
statement: understand the principle of a potential divider circuit

title: Potentiometer for comparing pd
statement: recall and use the principle of the potentiometer as a means of comparing potential differences

title: Galvanometer in null methods
statement: understand the use of a galvanometer in null methods

title: Thermistors and LDRs in potential dividers
statement: explain the use of thermistors and light-dependent resistors in potential dividers to provide a potential difference that is dependent on temperature and light intensity

title: Evidence for the nucleus from scattering
statement: infer from the results of the α-particle scattering experiment the existence and small size of the nucleus

title: Simple nuclear atom model
statement: describe a simple model for the nuclear atom to include protons, neutrons and orbital electrons

title: Nucleon number and proton number
statement: distinguish between nucleon number and proton number

title: Isotopes
statement: understand that isotopes are forms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei

title: Nuclide notation
statement: understand and use the notation ${}^{A}_{Z}X$ for the representation of nuclides

title: Conservation in nuclear processes
statement: understand that nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes

title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
statement: describe the composition, mass and charge of α-, β- and γ-radiations (both β– (electrons) and β+ (positrons) are included)

title: Antiparticles and the positron
statement: understand that an antiparticle has the same mass but opposite charge to the corresponding particle, and that a positron is the antiparticle of an electron

title: Neutrinos in beta decay
statement: state that (electron) antineutrinos are produced during β– decay and (electron) neutrinos are produced during β+ decay

title: Discrete versus continuous decay energies
statement: understand that α-particles have discrete energies but that β-particles have a continuous range of energies because (anti)neutrinos are emitted in β-decay

title: Writing radioactive decay equations
statement: represent α- and β-decay by a radioactive decay equation of the form ${}^{238}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}Th + {}^{4}_{2}\alpha$

title: The unified atomic mass unit
statement: use the unified atomic mass unit (u) as a unit of mass

title: Quarks and their flavours
statement: understand that a quark is a fundamental particle and that there are six flavours (types) of quark: up, down, strange, charm, top and bottom

title: Charges of quarks and antiquarks
statement: recall and use the charge of each flavour of quark and understand that its respective antiquark has the opposite charge (no knowledge of any other properties of quarks is required)

title: Quark composition of protons and neutrons
statement: recall that protons and neutrons are not fundamental particles and describe protons and neutrons in terms of their quark composition

title: Baryons and mesons
statement: understand that a hadron may be either a baryon (consisting of three quarks) or a meson (consisting of one quark and one antiquark)

title: Quark changes in beta decay
statement: describe the changes to quark composition that take place during β– and β+ decay

title: Electrons and neutrinos as leptons
statement: recall that electrons and neutrinos are fundamental particles called leptons
